author: Elastic
rule.description:
This rule identifies the first segmentation fault, SIGSEGV, signal 11 termination, or Windows access-violation status
observed in web-server error logs for a host during the configured history window. An unexpected web-server crash can
indicate attempted exploitation of a memory-safety vulnerability, including attempts that fail before code execution,
although software defects and resource problems can produce the same behavior.
false_positives:
Web-server, runtime, module, extension, or application defects can legitimately crash a worker after an upgrade,
    configuration change, or unusual request.

Stress tests, fault-injection exercises, fuzzing, and authorized vulnerability testing may intentionally trigger
    segmentation faults or access violations.
rule.name: First Occurrence of a Web Server Segmentation Fault
rule.note:
## Triage and analysis

### Investigating First Occurrence of a Web Server Segmentation Fault

A segmentation fault is a memory-access violation that terminates a process or worker. A first-seen crash in an
internet-facing service deserves prompt review because memory-corruption exploit attempts frequently terminate workers
even when exploitation fails. This alert does not prove exploitation or successful code execution.

### Possible investigation steps

- Identify the affected `host.id`, process or worker identifier, signal or exception value, web-server module, and complete
  error text. Determine whether one worker or the entire service terminated.
- Review requests immediately preceding the crash, including `source.ip`, URL, method, status, content type, body size,
  cookies, and user agent. Recover the original client from trusted edge logs when a proxy or container bridge is present.
- Correlate the crash with fatal PHP errors, malformed multipart requests, repeated HTTP 500 responses, worker churn, and
  known vulnerability signatures such as the PHP2Shell memory-exhaustion pattern.
- Review endpoint telemetry for a core dump, unexpected child processes, file writes, outbound connections, privilege
  changes, or persistence after the crash.
- Determine whether a recent deployment, package upgrade, native extension, security test, or resource-pressure event can
  explain the fault. Preserve a core dump and relevant binaries when available.

### False positive analysis

- Native modules, language runtimes, drivers, and third-party extensions can contain non-security defects that crash a
  web worker. Recurrent crashes with the same stack after an approved change may be operational rather than adversarial.
- Do not broadly exclude a host solely because it has a known stability issue; use a narrow exception for the understood
  message, module, version, or maintenance window.

### Response and remediation

- Remove a repeatedly crashing or potentially exploited server from public traffic and preserve volatile and on-disk
  evidence before restarting or rebuilding it.
- Patch the web server, runtime, application, and native extensions. If exploitation cannot be ruled out, rebuild from a
  trusted image and rotate credentials and secrets accessible to the service account.
- Block confirmed malicious origins at the edge and hunt for the same crash signature and follow-on behavior on peer hosts.
rule.query:
agent.id:* and
event.dataset:("apache.error" or "nginx.error" or "apache_tomcat.catalina" or "apache_tomcat.localhost") and
message:(
  segfault or SIGSEGV or (Segmentation and fault) or (signal and 11) or "0xc0000005" or "c0000005" or "3221225477"
)
